segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We are glad that you came as we begin, what is your name in English?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: My name is Doris Shell in English.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: Geyhuneg in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where were you born?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: I was just born at the house. They just find me at Bunch.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you just grow up there?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: That’s where I grew. They called it Jegi when they talked about it in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What were your parents’ names?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: My dad's name is Dirthrower and my mom's name was Uyosda. Her name is Winnie Mae Vann.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many were in your family?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: There were six of us, but we lost one brother.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did all of you speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: All of us speak Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What were your parents’ names?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: Gad(a) Udeg(a) - Dirthrower Vann and Uyosd(a) - Winnie Mae Vann.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did you go to school?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: I started at Kentucky in first grade. When I started seventh grade, they took us to Greasy and closed our school down.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about the rest?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: When I finished eighth grade there, I went to Cave Springs and finished the twelfth grade, and from there I went to Bacone for two years. And then I came back to Northeastern and went to school there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What do you remember growing up?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: A lot of things you could talk about how I grew up. Like what?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Whatever you can think of.

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: Whatever I can think of. We used to pick strawberries when it was summertime. We used to pick strawberries. I haven’t picked beans, not myself, but Mom and Dad have. They were bean pickers, but personally, I didn’t pick them. I was always babysitting other children that were growing up. My siblings, I was watching them. They would take us to the creek in the evenings. When we got back from playing late in the evening, we would go to the creek. We would take soap and towels. We would play in the water, then, when Mom thought we were done playing, we would clean up at the creek. We would make our hair real soapy, and our bodies. Then, when we got back, it was time to go to sleep. We grew up doing that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Didn’t your dad raise strawberries?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: Yes, it was about an acre in size where he raised strawberries. But just our family, my uncles and aunts and their children picked the strawberries. My mother was an only child. She did not have any siblings, but my dad had plenty of siblings. There were nine of them. They helped – we all worked together picking strawberries. We would pick the strawberries, and Dad would take them to town and sell them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Your aunts and uncles you were talking about, did they speak fluent Cherokee?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: They spoke fluent Cherokee. They didn’t hardly speak any English. My grandmother and grandfather – my dad's parents. My grandmother's name was Susani. She was 108 years old when she passed away and my grandfather was 102. Diganotsatli and Susani was their names. But mom's mom passed in ‘73. She was 82 years old.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you are married. You are married to a good-looking man.

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: I am married, but I don’t know if he is good-looking. Or that’s what I think.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many children are you raising?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: Two of our own, that is our biological. A 45-year-old boy that is the oldest and a girl that is 38. And the rest, there are four children: two girls and two boys. We have two that we took in and raised. All the children that we have are seven years apart. Our oldest son is named Keith. When he was seven years old, we had a girl that is our own. Candy is…Uyosdi is her name. The boy's name is Tsigili. We were given a girl. She was seven years old. A little boy we had, just came. He had just come from the hospital. He had been born only about three days. I asked his mom if I could take him, and his mom asked me if I could take him. We took him and adopted him. That boy was going on about six and a half years, then our three-year-old granddaughter we struggled to get, so also, she was given to us and we raised her. When she was 26, then some little ones, the girl that was my granddaughter, was taken by the DHS. Then we struggled to get her, but her and her brother came to us. In all, we have raised six children.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Let’s back up. Tell us about your experience going to school at Kentucky.

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: There were 32 of us students. My mother was the cook at that school. There were two teachers, one was teaching first through fourth, and the other was teaching fifth to eighth. That school was just one building; they just halved it. There were 32 of us going to school there. That is why we lost that school for a while. They were wanting some of it to go towards Cave Springs and some of it towards Greasy, but our parents had to say where they were going to send us children. I had never rode in a bus until I was in the eighth grade – that was the first time I rode in a bus. We walked a little bit, but we lived just a little ways up the hill. We didn’t have to walk very far.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did you think about riding in the bus?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: It was strange. I had seen children riding in a bus. I never thought I would have to do that. I used to think it was going to be at Cave Springs, but I thought I will be older, I don’t have to think about it right now. I used to think all the time. But when they sent us to Greasy on the bus. And our uncle was driving the bus at that time. It was easy for us. We were all speaking in Cherokee. We were all Cherokee that lived and went to school there in Kentucky. There were about three whites, but we never thought that they are white. They did the same thing as us Cherokee natives were doing, those children. They were used to it, and they were picking up what we were saying.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did y’all do at that school, as far as doing things?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: Like what? We did not have a gym. We did not play basketball, but we played softball. It was good. We were able to play at three schools. The teachers would take us when we had to play ball. Also, my mom worked there and cooked for us and took us, ‘cause it would be in the evening when we would play.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So y’all had enough to play ball.

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: The boys and girls were together for us, but so were those others. Brushy was one of them. They were the same way. And also Skelly was the same way.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Y’all went that far?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: Sometimes and sometimes they came their self.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did y’all play when they came?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: Just there, in the front of the school. We just had papers laying there we used for bases. The bats and gloves belonged to us. They did not belong to the school.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Tell us a little more about what your family has been through.

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: We were made to work, like the boys, they had to feed the cows, pigs, and horses and cut wood and us girls, my sister, we were nine almost 10 years old apart. She seemed like a baby to me, all the time. She had not hardly done anything. But when I was nine, I began to cook for my dad. I would get up at 4:30 in the morning and cook breakfast for him, then I would fix him something for lunch. He would take a lunch bucket. When I came back from school, I would lay down and sleep for a little while, then I would go back to school. Then, when I came back in the afternoon, I would have to cook again. You have seen those milk carton crates? I would stand on one of those and cook. We used a wood cook stove to cook. We used a fire to cook. When it came time to wash dishes, I would stand on that and put those dish pans on top. They call them dikvhewidi.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Tell us a little bit about your grandfather that used to live with y’all.

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: I had been born two weeks; I don’t remember when that old man came. His name was Galinvdi. Mom said he asked her and Dad if he could live with them. He used to go around preaching. It’s called Briartown, by Vian, close to Porum. We used to go there and take him. And also, there at Bunch, he pastored there, too, I don’t remember. The first and third Sunday, we went to one church. The second and fourth Sunday we went to another church to preach, when we were growing up. And like I’m saying, I hadn’t been born but two weeks when he came to live with us. We thought of him as our grandpa, but he was related to Mom or Dad. But we loved him. That old man taught us a lot. He was the one who started feeding the hogs. But as far as giving them water or other work, the boys had that to do. Sometimes he had a little wagon, and he used that to feed them pigs. He had them in there, and I would get on top and go with him. When I would tell him I wanted to go with him, he would put me on there. I would go with him to feed the pigs. And there was a pond there and that’s where he would get water, and give to the pigs. If it wasn’t for that, the boys would do. But the boys wouldn’t let me on there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I guess they thought it was too heavy.

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: Because they were mean. But that’s all I did and for the rest I just had to cook. And after we ate, there were eight – no nine of us in that family. You would have to wash all the dishes, and I was the only one standing around doing all the dishes. When I would finish that, I would go to bed before eight and I would already be tired. That’s just how we all lived, and sometimes I went and helped feed the cows. And when we thought we would do something different, and I’ve also hunted. I would go coon hunting with the boys, and I would hold the flashlight. The boys would be walking in the front. They couldn’t walk very fast because I was too slow. Because I had the light they couldn’t go too far, they would gripe at me because I wouldn’t hurry up. I didn’t feel like it. We hunted coon and I was scared. I didn’t want to see a snake. They looked after me good. They never would mistreat me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did your dad do?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: At first, that’s all. The first time, that’s all I remember. When I was little, they used to pick cotton, Mom and Dad. I remember I would just be on top. That’s all I remember – them picking cotton. I remember it good when they were picking beans. I was babysitting, I wasn’t picking beans. When he finished that, Dad worked on the railroad, and he had to travel far. He quit that and did that for a little while, then he started building bridges and worked on the road. He did that until he retired. I think he started from Oktah, toward Oklahoma City. Oktah to Russellville, he built bridges on I-40 road. He built all those bridges on that road. We grew up him just doing that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did your mom do?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: She worked at Kentucky as a cook. And when they sent us to Greasy, she found work out there. She worked as a teacher’s aide in the second grade, helping the teacher for work.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did she not teach a little bit of Cherokee? Was she not a bilingual aide?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: That’s why she was in there on the Title 7 Program, I think that’s what they called it back then. She was a Cherokee teacher and there was quite a few Cherokee students. There at Greasy there were three or four women that were hired that made a lot of books at that time to teach with. Whatever they could find and different things they could teach with. She was hired through Agnes Cowen’s bilingual program.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you went to Canada, where did you work and tell me a little bit about what you seen there?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: Belfonte ᏧᏲᎱᏒ ᏗᏢ hired me in the year of 84. When I started at that school, it wasn’t very long after I started, I taught Cherokee there, too, in the evenings. I was scared to go through Low Gap, they called it, so Dad always went with me in the evenings. He didn’t want me to go by myself. I don’t know if I had only started about a year and the boss called me in and said I was fired. I said, "What did I do, what’s the reason?” He said nothing. “On what grounds you want to fire me for?” “I want you to do something else.” “What is it?” “The program that you’re on, I’m on the same one, Title 7 Program, bilingual program. That woman is leaving and I have to fire you because I want you to fill her position.” “I’m not able to do that, I’ve never done that.” And so, “Go home because I already fired you." “So, when are you gonna call me back? But you have to have a reason to fire me.” But he said, “Come back tomorrow, and be the boss.” “That soon?” “Go home and talk to your husband and come back tomorrow.” I didn’t know they were going to do that.

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: The first time I got on a plane, they sent me to Canada. There was a few of us and one of us was Harlene Green. She was hired to run that bilingual program. Me and my mom were together at that time on that program, but she was at Greasy and the other one was Joanne Wafford. We all were all together when we went. It was scary to get on the plane for the first time. I was thinking, “What’s going to happen?” Because there was a man sitting on this side and there wasn’t anyone sitting on this side. They said y’all are going to be full, so you can’t sit in a different seat. And Mom and Joanne was sitting in the very back. And Harlene was in the front. When we took off, I was thinking. “What’s going to happen?” When the plane took off, I said “Oow!” and grabbed that man's leg. He said, “It’s OK, honey.” We took off pretty good. And that…what do you call that when you get to a different country?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Was it a visa?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: No, it wasn’t a visa.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it a passport?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: No, it wasn’t a passport. I forgot what they called it. They check from America to that country. We had to go through that. Just a minute, I’ll remember. It’s Customs. We went through that. We made it good going there. When we got there they asked us if we got Canada’s money. We just had America’s money. A woman came and said, “I have a son who is 16 years old and he will take you all to the bank. You can exchange your money there,” they told us. We left and made it to the bank and exchanged our money, then we went on. None of us had ever been there. “If y’all give me a dollar, I will take y’all to look around” and quickly we gave him a dollar. That boy didn’t want to go to school, and that was his excuse. That’s what he told his mom, but he took us around and it was really good. It was strange how they did things over there because the car drivers had to go through customs. They taught them courtesy before they would give them a license. If someone was standing there, like a pedestrian, us we wait for a car to go by before we cross, but there in Canada they don’t. The car stops and the person walking, walks by. They had more laws for them to go by. All the cars quit and stop. They went by – they would go on. We got to a Walmart. “Can you take us there?” They had a small Walmart. We were going there and he put on the blinker, and it was blinking so we could park over there. And a little car was coming toward us and went quickly around us. That car was from the US and that boy was going to get out. Quickly he put that car in park and he said, "I’m gonna beat that guy up,” he said. I said, “Why are you going to do that?” “I already claimed to park there. But they don’t have a right to do that. Once I have my signal light on, it belongs to me,” he said. I told him, “Stay in.” I thought we all were going to be in jail. He settled down and I told him, “There’s another spot over there we can park." I was the only one speaking and those old women were just sitting there not saying nothing. But when it came time to eat, they asked Mom what she wanted to eat and she said iced tea. He said what? She said iced tea and he said, “We don’t have anything like that ma’am,” he told her. “You don’t have tea?” “Yeah, we have some, but it’s boiled.” They didn’t put ice in their tea. And I just asked for water – I don’t like tea. Joanne was doing something strange, that other one that was with Mom. She asked for it warm. They told her, “Warm water?” She was putting salt in her drinking water. I asked her why she was doing that and she said, “I always do that, put salt in my drinking water.”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She didn’t say why?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: She didn’t say. She just said she liked it like that. That’s just what she knew. But when we were coming back in that plane, we were in Salt Lake City, Utah. It was the first time I seen where they look to see if you have anything on you. There was a girl over there and something made a sound where they look for things. Harlene said to be looking over there. They took that woman's clothes off and they told her to go into here, into this little building. And they put her in there. She stayed in there. They made her take all her clothes off. She was trying to hide what she had. Something that wasn’t good. When we seen her again, she had …

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Handcuffs.

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: She had handcuffs on. They handcuffed her and took her. But her clothes were scattered everywhere. And those people that clean up, had to put those gloves on and put those things in a trash bag and took it all. It was strange to me. I’ve never seen anything like that before. When we were coming back, me and Mom made it through good. To get back to the US, we had to go through Customs again. We were waiting. “We’ll be home here a little later," me and Mom was saying. Then the intercom sounded and said, “Doris Shell come back through customs." “Why?!” I’m thinking. Mom said, “Sis, what did you do?” I said, “I don’t know!” I was scared. And again, someone from the US took me back towards Canada and we almost went around. And over this way, Joanne Wallford was standing there. I said, “What?” Joanne was doing this [gestures] shaking her head. “What is it?” I told them. They said, “We can’t get her to talk to us.” I said, “What happened, Joanne?” I told her. “I’m scared," she said. They scared her. “She just froze on us,” the guy said. All she had to do was show them her ID. “I didn’t know what they were saying to me,” she said. “It’s just scaring you now and we’re going back to the US.”

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about, you said you were taught by your grandpa. Tell me about what he taught you.

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: The way we did things, as I remember, when there’s a new moon, there’s a new moon as we say it. We were made to go out of the house. We had to go look at that new moon. And next month take us again, you led us through good this month. We'll see each other next month and tell your grandfather, ‘Hi’. We were standing outside, talking to it. All six of us were standing there doing that. No…it was five, ‘cause that youngest one. I was 18, almost 19, when they was born. It was quite a while later when they were born. My sister was born after us. Our sister who they treated like a baby was 10 when our brother was born. It was me who raised him. My mother was experiencing the change of life, as they say. It was that she was experiencing when my brother was born. One night she was whipping him and telling him to be quiet. I went in there and asked Mom what he was doing. “Having a fit,” she told me. “Mom, he’s just little, maybe he’s hungry,” I told her. “Don’t tell me what to do! I’m a grown-up.” “Let me pick him up for a little while,” I told her. I picked him up and she slapped me. Dad was laying down. “Why did you do that?” he told her. “She’s taking this baby from me,” she told him. “Just for a little while, she told you,” he told her. Dad told me to take the baby. They were having a talk. They were in the room. I don’t know what happened. Ever since then I raised that boy, Gary. He was always standing around next to me. When I went out on dates, we didn’t hardly go anywhere ourselves. But the other thing the old man taught us, if someone passed away, to go over there and help, “since y’all are girls, take things, because they need it.” When we would get there and someone was sick, that one had to come outside. “If y’all had been to a place where someone has passed. When y’all come in, they can come in, that sick can come in.” That’s just the way we was taught. If we were sick and we knew it, and Mom and Dad didn’t really take to places like that where someone had passed. They didn’t take us anywhere where someone had passed. I was 13 when my grandpa passed, my mom’s father figure passed away. That was the first time I'd ever been to a funeral, at that time. All the family would go out. We would go in. We had been to a place like that. That’s what they taught us, growing up. When we were eating, they would tell us not to be singing. “It’s not good to be singing when you were eating,” they would tell us. They would teach us girls what we’re supposed to do, “Because someday you’re gonna have your own families.” That’s what they taught us, and that’s what I learned from. Some of what they told me I forgot. Sometimes we would turn the TV off and listen to Grandpa talking about things. We enjoyed listening to him telling us things.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And now that you said that, do you remember anything he said that you can tell us that he told you?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: Some of it, some of it I remember. He talked about things that happened to him and he always talked about himself. I can’t hardly talk about, if he talked about some kids, he called them “cotton heads”, white people lived back behind us. He said their names were Ballard. They had several children, and they lived in poor conditions. He canned, but I never seen him do that. He didn’t do that when he lived at Mom’s. He had things that he had canned. I guess his wife was still living back then. So, he said he just gave him things to eat. “Those poor kids,” he said. There were seven or eight of them would go by and they were skinny kids. But one time he said, "I’m going to set a trap for someone; they were bothering me,” he said. “I’m going to set a trap,” I thought. We left and it was towards the evening, he said, “Tonight I’m going to catch that person for bothering me and then I fixed some medicine,” he said. “It was late at night," he said. “I heard an owl making a sound and a call. I was thinking ‘It’s here now’,” he said. “And I went and got a gun. [boom] I shot at it, but I missed it, but it came back again later. I thought it came back to bother me again. [boom] I shot it! It was flying and I shot it in the wing. It went down," he said. “When it went down, it said, ‘Let me go, let me go!' A bird was laying there. ‘Let me go.’ I said, ‘Go home and don’t ever bother me!’ It was laying there and I left. I didn’t help it, ‘cause I thought, ‘You’ve been bothering me a lot.’ After four days, an old lady came and there was something wrong with her arm.” He used to just talk about things like that. His self… “I was flirting with him, they were flirting with me. They were flirting with me,” he said. ‘I didn’t know who it was,’ he said.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is that the only place? Where did you go after you finished at Belfonte?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: Worked there for 17 years at Belfonte. When that bilingual program ended, I took a break for a little while and drew unemployment. When I thought, “I have to go back to work now,” there was a place in Sallisaw that did sewing, making jackets and sweatshirts and things like that they made. And I got a job there…but wait. Before I started there, I got a job at People Inc. For a little while, it was a nighttime job. I cared for an old man and an old woman. I used to look after them. I worked there about a week. I didn’t like it. I wasn’t hardly sleeping in the daytime. I was raising children and I had to do some things in the daytime, and I would just sleep for a little while and then I would have to go back to work overnight and then work all night. I got a job at the sewing place with my oldest son. We worked there for a little while. While I was working there, I applied for the housing authority. I worked there for about three months, then I started at the housing authority. I worked there for seven years. Then there was an opening at Cherokee Nation, at community services, and I’ve been at the Cherokee Nation since then.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What are you doing right now?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: The advanced speaker students are the ones I have now and there are five of them. I tried to go everywhere east and…

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: West.

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: West and north. Everywhere. And we’d go to Stilwell, Belfonte, Spavinaw – I don’t know what that is in Cherokee. We go all the way over there.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: ᏧᏍᏓᎾᎸ.

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: What ᏧᏍᏓᎾᎸ?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: ᏧᏍᏓᎾᎸ.

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: And here in Tahlequah. We're chasing the different dialects. They have different ways of saying things, but they all talk about the same things. Like, where we’re from, like Cherry Tree, Bell, you can easily tell. It’s different. You can quickly tell if somebody is from a different place. Toward the north, people from Jay. They're fast talkers. Toward Bell, they talk slow. That one student said I was just like this [gestures] I was thinking, “Is he finished?” And then he would start up again and start talking. And from Cherry Tree it’s kind of like a song. High, low, high, low is how they talk. Us Greasy people talk the best. Not for real, I was just saying that when this school first started. Me and my brother and ᏓᏰᏂ first started this. It wasn’t a program, it was called a pilot program when we first started. We started teaching them, we taught them for two years, ᏎᎷ sitting there was one of them that we taught. Two of them…no three have been through there where I taught.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did they get better at talking?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: If they would talk, because they’re not talking, not until I ask them something, then they’ll speak. When y’all are talking to each other, y’all need to speak Cherokee to each other, but then they throw around English. You have to get onto them like kids sometimes.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Let’s back up for a little while. When you were growing up, what was your thoughts, did y’all think y’all were poor?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: I never really thought about us being poor. We were really sheltered, they call it. We didn’t see other people doing things. We didn’t know. We never did go to like, movies. We never did that. We didn’t have time, we didn’t have time, not that much. We had too much to do; they made us do a lot. And it was too far for us to go to town. I didn’t realize that our parents worked that hard. We didn’t get what we wanted but if we needed it, we got it. We were not in need. One time I remember on Sunday, Grandpa and Grandma would take us to Greasy, my dad’s parents’ house. When we get there, they would say, “Uncle D, give us some money!” And he would take it out and give it to them. If they would say, “Uncle D, I want this!” he would give it to them. One time I asked Dad. “It bothers me what you do.” He said, “What is it?” “When the others say, ‘Uncle D, I want this’, you just give it to them." I told him, “You don’t treat us like that.” He said, “Sister, those over there are having it hard. They don’t get the things that you get. That’s why I give it to them. Like the things you have, they don’t have and I buy it. I don’t have to give you the money to buy it,” he told me. He griped at me. Just because I asked some things. And really growing up I didn’t think that we had it hard. My mom was canning. She liked to can to preserve things for us to eat. She would make our dresses herself. She never bought them in town. Those ugly, dirty black and white shoes we were wearing. One time on Easter Sunday, I remember I was wearing some like that. Another girl came and she was wearing high heels. I was really wanting them from her. I said, "Mom, I want some like that.” She said, “What?” I was wearing a dress she made herself. “Shoes like that.” “You’re wearing some,” she said. I was hiding my shoes. I said, “I know, but she’s wearing pretty shoes.” “But sister, she’s not going to wear them very long, but you’re going to wear yours all the time.” It was a long time until they got too little. Them shoes did not tear up. It wasn’t until they got too little, we got different ones. That was all I knew. Nowadays I can’t have a lot. You know how nowadays women have lots of shoes? It’s not like that. I just think, “I have shoes." I feel different about it now, but growing up I didn’t think about it. Worked hard feeding us and raising us.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about when it came time to kill hogs? Tell us a little bit about that for a little while.

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: My dad's brother was named ᏬᏱ and Dad would go get him. I didn’t pay that much attention, but from what I knew as a child, when Woyi came to the house, he was gonna kill a hog, that’s how I felt. When we got there all the time, he would come running and I would lock the doors, and he would say, “I’m going with you.” I would say, “You’re not coming with us,” because I didn’t want him killing the hogs. I didn’t think Dad was going to get him to kill hogs, because there were several that came. They would kill a hog. They would have fattened it up. I didn’t go where they killed it. It wasn’t until they brought it to where they scraped it, that’s when I would see it already dead. They would drag it around for a long time, boiling that water, scraping that hog. Then they would hang it up and the guts would fall out. Now, I don’t know the reason for the part that it uses the bathroom with... Real quick...

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: A boy/a male.

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: If it was a boy/male. They would hang it [testicles] from a tree, and they would wrap around there [the private parts]. I don’t know the reason why. I never asked. They would tell him, “You already did it, someone else is going to have to do it.” I guess there was a reason they did that, I think nowadays. I never asked. Sometimes I think it would have been good if I asked, but I never did ask anyone. And also, when they got done scraping it, the guts… I have helped clean the guts before, but I didn’t like helping them do that and the liver. I would take them into the house, and I would rinse them off and take everything off of them. Dad would lay the pig down and put it in four quarters and put it in the refrigerator for a little while. When he would come back at nighttime, he would start cutting it up again. And when he would cut it up, we had a white paper and I would wrap it up and put that meat in the freezer.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you know why he put the meat in the freezer for a little while?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: He told me that chilling the meat made it firm, which made it easier to cut. When the meat was still warm, it would stretch and be harder to handle.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you like them chitlins?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: I didn’t.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: I liked them though.

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: My brother Roger liked them though, but he didn’t help clean them. If he would’ve liked cleaning them, he wouldn’t have. I didn’t try them, I didn’t want to try them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Tell us a little bit about Roger.

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: I might start crying. Just every little thing he would tell you, like, it was true. He would find something quickly to tell. He was like what they call a storyteller. There’s no telling how long he would tell a story if someone was listening. And also in English, when he realized—or, learned the words. There’s no telling how many times he would use it sometimes it’d make sense and then sometimes it wouldn’t make sense. I’ll tell you all one of his stories. They sent us to California one time; they said they wanted someone to cook hog meat. I made the bread and we was together with Charlie Soap. We went, they took us and when we got there, a black woman was walkin’ toward us. She was wearing a hat with feathers in it. She was doing this [gestures] and I was doing the stirring. We called Roger, Sonny. Sonny was standing there stirring the meat. Charlie was standing on this side thinking about getting it out of the pot. So, she came and said, “Sir, sir.” She did this [gestures] and said, “What are you doing?” He said, “I’m cooking hog meat." She said, “Are you Cherokee?” -- “Yes, I’m Cherokee.” But I’m gonna use a little English here. That woman said, “I'd like to know how to become Cherokee.” Sonny already knew what he was going to say. Quickly, Sonny said, “If you’re moving on the road and you see a turtle,” he told her. “That turtle has to be coming from the east and heading towards the west,” he told her. “But not coming from the west to east, that won’t be good,” he told her. “But you can’t do it unless it’s early in the morning. Then you get that turtle, quickly, and cover it up. And if your hand gets wet, wash your face with all of that. And wash your face with all of that.” And Charlie Soap was standing over here on this side, “Doris, isn’t that pee?” he said. I said, “Be quiet, Charlie!” and I faced the other way. “Oh, is that right, sir?” that black lady said. Sonny kept a straight face and didn’t ever laughed. “I’m gonna have to try that, sir,” she was saying. Charlie yelled, “Roger!” As soon as he said that, Sonny started laughing. Boy, he pranked that black woman. He was mischievous, that boy.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about that girl he was raising, can you tell me about that?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: All of my siblings have children that they adopted. We have adopted children. My sister is the only one who didn’t want one (adopted). The rest of us and the boys have children who were adopted. But the oldest one, Sonny, we already had the first one we adopted. His name was Tim. We already had him. Our oldest daughter’s friend was named Justine. She was raising her child in a poor way. She would always bring it to the house and stay all night. Her grandfather made a mistake. And then them kids had to be taken away. They didn’t take them away right then, but they were talking about they were going to do that. And then the mother was not able to raise two or three children. And then Sonny adopted that boy and said, “I will take it in. It would be too hard for y’all, because y’all already have one.” And Roger already had two kids. A boy and a girl. But just anytime soon, they can talk to that girl, they said. And he didn’t hardly know anything at school. He hadn’t hardly been to school. They told her, “You need to do homework, because that’s the only way you’re going to learn.” They went about two or three weeks and that girl wasn’t hardly doing any homework. “Justine, sit down here,” he told her. She came and sat down. She was sitting there like this. He said, “Do this. Look! [sounds] Your head is making a sound because it has water in it. Do this, do this. I'll have a wash rag” and he laid it up there. He and his wife, they had already figured out what they were going to do. And his wife had another one. They changed places quickly. He said, “Look.” He laid it up there, and it was wet. “Look, we're getting the water out of your ear.” And that little girl looked at him, and he said, “Now you’re going to start learning!” And she started learning. She believed it was true because water came out of her head. That’s how smart he was to figure things out. He was funny though. At church one time, what was it…? It was something… evolution. The Bibles we have wasn’t like that, “We didn’t come from monkeys!” He was teaching Sunday school. “God made us,” he was saying. I didn’t hear it for myself. The others were talking about it. “There ain’t no reason!” He said, “Erection.” -- “What they talk about at school,” he said. And his daughter said, “Dad! Evolution!" she told him. “I need to practice that word,” he said. That’s the way we lived. We thought things were funny. That oldest boy was two years old when I was born. “You was given the best present when you were two years old," I told him. “It was me that was given to you,” I told him. But his wife, when we got married, his wife and my husband has the same birthday. I have the same birthday as Roger and Patty and Charlie had the same birthday. And our kids… I had a child first, I had a boy and he had a girl. The second time we started to have kids, I took my sister-in-law to the hospital. While I was there, I had my baby, same day our kids were born. 17 … No … 11 hours apart. And then, Charlie was a preacher and he was a deacon and they were ordained the same day. “We're doing a lot of the same stuff, ain’t it?” I told him.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is that all you have?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s all I have.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I’m gonna ask you this. You teach these students here, what do you think is going to happen to the language?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: I’m just going to tell you the truth. They're not going to talk like us. They’re just going to talk a learned language. They’re going to talk like that kind of language. I think the way we speak it, we’re going to lose it. I can’t hardly speak to those in immersion. The reason is because they have made words, and I don’t know that. Like a computer, I don’t know. They call it “you save it," but I don’t know the things that they name them. And also, in the Bible it says the color purple, ᎤᏪᏘᎨ it says. And they say ᎠᏓᎭᎵᎨ. It’s going to be like that, the way they talk, I believe. If we don’t lose it, they gonna start talking like that. If we’re still alive when they grow up, we’re not going to understand each other. That’s what I think.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about the things that we see, what are the things the ones behind are going to see?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: What I think, we are heading in a bad direction. They’re going to see starvation. As for love, it’s not going to be true. As well as siblings and families. Even now, some children have nothing to do with their parents. Parents don’t have nothing to do with their kids. That’s what is going to happen, I think. Families don’t see each other very much or visit each other. We have put away visiting each other. If someone is sick, we will just say, “Huh." We would not go see them. A long time ago, when we were growing up, our parents would be going to help out. It’s not like that these days.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What are they going to see here on Earth then?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: They’re going to see bad things.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I’m talking about things that exist now.

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: What things that exist. Technology? For us we’re not going to know anything about it. There are too many things changing these days. Things are faster. And there, they’re losing patience. They can’t hardly wait. When it’s time to eat, what do they do? They just microwave it. We don’t know things like that, but we have learned. And we’re going to learn, if we live long enough, that things are going to change. I believe that someday there aren’t going to be teachers in places like this. We’re just going to be seeing each other in places like this. That’s what I think is going to happen.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Maybe you’re thinking, “This is what you want to say to them.” We're finishing up now.

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: If you are able, write things down as you learn them. Share those words and teachings with others — especially with students, learners, and the generations coming up behind us. Some people still remember the old language our parents spoke, and it is important to pass that knowledge along while we can. I would like to tell those coming up after us: make an effort to love one another.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Is that it?

segments.speaker: doris-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I appreciate you.
